headline: US launches heavy strikes on Iran as Middle East conflict widens — gold surges to $4,097 while the ASX slipped 0.78% today and Australian inflation eases to 3.8%, reducing rate hike fears.

movers.name: Pilbara Minerals
movers.note: PLS bounced strongly today after reporting 31% growth in its June 2026 quarter — a genuinely solid operational update that reassured investors the lithium miner is improving its output. There's also growing interest in lithium for grid-scale energy storage (not just EVs), which is a longer-term tailwind for the sector.

movers.name: Alphabet Inc. (Google)
movers.note: Google edged up last night in a broadly soft session — likely some rotation into quality tech names as investors weighed Microsoft's earnings. One fund manager made headlines calling Google 'the best business in the world' after buying it at 15x earnings, which may have added to sentiment.

movers.name: Vanguard Emerging Markets ETF
movers.note: VGE crept slightly higher today, a modest positive in a down session for the broader ASX. Emerging markets have been quietly benefiting from a softer USD and ongoing demand from Asia.

movers.name: Microsoft
movers.note: Microsoft dipped slightly last night despite a very strong earnings report — Azure cloud revenue hit $39.3B (beating analyst estimates of $38.2B) and cloud growth hit its fastest pace since 2022. The small pullback likely reflects 'sell the news' after a big run-up into earnings. The underlying result was excellent.

movers.name: Vanguard Diversified High Growth ETF
movers.note: VDHG slipped today largely because of weakness in US equities (it holds significant US exposure) and a soft ASX session. No specific news — just general market risk-off sentiment as the Iran conflict rattled global markets.

movers.name: Global X AI ETF
movers.note: GXAI pulled back today as the NASDAQ had a rough session last night (down 1.74%). AI-themed ETFs tend to move with high-growth tech, so when the NASDAQ drops, GXAI follows. No specific negative news for the AI sector — the pullback is market-driven.

movers.name: Take-Two Interactive
movers.note: Take-Two edged slightly lower last night in a weak NASDAQ session. No specific news — the broader market sell-off, driven by Middle East tensions pushing investors to safer assets, weighed on gaming stocks.

movers.name: Vanguard US Total Market ETF
movers.note: VTS fell today tracking the S&P 500's overnight decline of 1.52%. US stocks fell last night as escalating US-Iran military conflict spooked investors and pushed money into safe havens like gold. This is the ASX-listed version of the US market, so it mirrors those moves.

watch_today.title: PLS.AX — best day in a while, but still deep in the red
watch_today.detail: Pilbara Minerals jumped 2.68% today after a strong June quarter (31% output growth). That's encouraging, but the position is still down 37.5% overall. For a long-term holder, today's move is a good sign the worst may be behind it — sit tight and let the lithium recovery play out. No reason to sell into strength here.

watch_today.title: MSFT — great earnings, small dip. Classic 'sell the news'
watch_today.detail: Microsoft reported blowout earnings last night — Azure cloud grew 43% and beat estimates, and overall cloud revenue hit $39.3B vs the $38.2B forecast. The stock slipped 0.71% anyway, which is a classic 'sell the news' reaction after a strong run-up. The underlying business is firing on all cylinders. Long-term case is rock solid — hold or consider adding on any further weakness.

watch_today.title: GXAI.AX — down today but AI tailwinds remain intact
watch_today.detail: The Global X AI ETF fell 1.01% today as the NASDAQ dropped 1.74% last night. The position is down 21.8% overall, which stings. However, the AI investment theme is very much alive — Microsoft's Azure AI growth at 43% is a direct positive for the sector. This is a long-term play; a single bad session doesn't change the story. Hold.

watch_today.title: Iran war escalation — watch for market volatility this week
watch_today.detail: The US launched a two-hour barrage of strikes on 'dozens of targets' in Iran overnight after an attempted attack on American troops. Jordan says it foiled an Iranian missile attack. This is a major escalation — oil is up, gold has surged to $4,097 (up 1.55%), and global stocks fell sharply. If conflict deepens further, expect more risk-off moves that will hit your US-heavy holdings (VTS, VDHG, GXAI) and could push oil and gold higher. Keep an eye on developments this week.

watch_today.title: Gold at $4,097 — your portfolio has no direct gold exposure
watch_today.detail: Gold surged 1.55% last night to $4,097 per ounce as investors fled to safe havens amid the Iran strikes. It's now up significantly over recent months. You have no direct gold exposure in your portfolio — just worth being aware of if you've been considering it as a diversifier. Informational only.

watch_today.title: VTS.AX — down 1.06% today, long-term case unchanged
watch_today.detail: VTS fell today tracking last night's S&P 500 drop of 1.52%. The US market sold off on Iran war fears, not any economic deterioration. The long-term case for broad US equities remains intact. This is noise for a buy-and-hold investor — sit tight.

world.summary: The Middle East is the dominant global story today — the US has launched major strikes on Iran, triggering sharp moves in oil and gold markets and raising fears of a widening regional war. Elsewhere, a Trump ally has been confirmed to lead US intelligence, and AI insiders are calling for guardrails on their own technology.

stories.title: US launches 'heavy' strikes on Iran after attempted attack on American troops
stories.why_it_matters: The US carried out a two-hour barrage of air strikes on dozens of targets across Iran overnight, in response to an Iranian-backed attack on American troops stationed in the region. Jordan separately revealed it intercepted an Iranian ballistic missile — a sign the conflict is spilling beyond Iran's borders. Gold immediately surged to $4,097 and oil ticked up to $85 a barrel as investors sought safety. This is the most significant direct US-Iran military exchange in years, and if it escalates further, it could destabilise oil supplies from the Gulf and send shockwaves through global markets.

stories.title: Senate confirms Jay Clayton as Director of National Intelligence
stories.why_it_matters: The US Senate has confirmed Jay Clayton — a former Wall Street regulator and close Trump ally — to lead the entire US intelligence community as Director of National Intelligence. The DNI oversees the CIA, NSA, and all 18 US spy agencies. Clayton has no intelligence background, which has raised eyebrows. This puts a loyalist in charge of the country's most sensitive national security information at a time when the US is militarily engaged with Iran — a combination that has foreign policy watchers paying close attention.

stories.title: Trump administration pushes Supreme Court to allow full implementation of mail-in voting executive order
stories.why_it_matters: The Trump administration and a coalition of states are asking the Supreme Court to let a presidential executive order on mail-in voting take full effect immediately, while legal challenges work through the courts. The order reportedly imposes stricter ID and documentation requirements for postal votes. Critics argue it will make voting harder for millions of Americans — particularly elderly, rural, and low-income voters. With US midterms approaching, the outcome of this case could significantly shape who gets to vote and how.

stories.title: War widens: new fronts erupting across the Middle East as Iran conflict escalates
stories.why_it_matters: Beyond the direct US-Iran strikes, the WSJ and AFR report that multiple new fronts are opening across the Middle East — with proxy conflicts in Syria, Iraq, Yemen and Lebanon all showing signs of renewed flare-ups linked to Iranian networks. Analysts are warning this could be the beginning of a broader regional war rather than a contained exchange. For Australian investors, a prolonged Middle East conflict means sustained pressure on oil prices (which feeds into fuel costs and inflation here) and continued demand for safe-haven assets like gold.

stories.title: 1,100 AI employees at OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta and Google call for development slowdown
stories.why_it_matters: More than 1,100 employees at the world's top AI companies — including OpenAI, Anthropic, Google and Meta — have signed a letter asking the US government to slow down AI development, specifically targeting AI that can write its own code (so-called 'recursive self-improvement'). OpenAI and Anthropic have formally backed the plan. Sam Altman visited Congress to discuss AI regulation this week. It's a striking moment: the people building AI are the ones saying 'slow down'. For investors in GOOG and holdings like GXAI, it signals that government guardrails on AI are coming — the question is just how strict they'll be.

markets.summary: A rough session globally — the S&P 500 fell 1.52% and the NASDAQ dropped 1.74% last night as the US-Iran military escalation spooked investors and pushed money into safe havens. Gold surged to $4,097 and oil ticked up. The ASX followed suit today, closing down 0.78%. The Aussie dollar slipped slightly to US$0.696.

indicators.name: ASX 200
indicators.note: Closed down today, dragged by global risk-off sentiment after US strikes on Iran overnight.

indicators.name: S&P 500
indicators.note: Fell sharply last night — investors moved to safety as the US-Iran conflict escalated into direct military strikes.

indicators.name: NASDAQ Composite
indicators.note: Tech stocks hit harder than the broader market last night, with the index dropping nearly 1.74% in the session.

indicators.name: Gold (WTI)
indicators.note: Gold surged to a new high as investors fled to safe havens amid the Iran strikes — up over $62 in a single session.

indicators.name: Crude Oil (WTI)
indicators.note: Oil ticked up on Middle East tensions — any further escalation near the Gulf could push prices significantly higher.

indicators.name: AUD/USD
indicators.note: The Aussie dollar slipped slightly — risk-off moves tend to push the AUD lower as investors move to the USD.

politics.summary: Australia's inflation rate has dropped to 3.8%, a bigger-than-expected fall that has markets abandoning bets on an RBA interest rate rise. Good news for mortgage holders and the broader economy.

stories.title: Inflation falls to 3.8% — mortgage holders 'dodge a bullet'
stories.why_it_matters: Australia's inflation rate fell to 3.8% in the latest quarterly reading, coming in softer than economists expected. The drop has caused traders to rapidly abandon bets that the Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) would raise interest rates — meaning if you have a mortgage, you've likely dodged another rate hike. The AFR reports that market pricing for an RBA rate rise has fallen sharply, with traders now believing rates have peaked. That's a real relief for households that have been squeezed by 13 rate rises since 2022.

stories.title: Traders axe RBA rate rise bets — 'everyone has to change their mind'
stories.why_it_matters: Financial markets moved quickly after the inflation data — bond traders and interest rate futures markets swung sharply away from pricing in any more RBA rate hikes. The AFR quoted analysts saying 'everyone has to change their mind' about the rate outlook. For investors, lower rates ahead are generally good for growth assets like shares and property. For anyone with variable-rate debt, this is a meaningful reprieve.

stories.title: Why the RBA still wants Australians to stay worried about inflation
stories.why_it_matters: Despite the good news on inflation, the RBA has been deliberately cautious about declaring victory — the bank wants households and businesses to keep expecting inflation to stay under control, because that expectation itself helps keep prices down (if everyone expects prices to keep rising, they demand higher wages, which pushes prices up further). The West Australian notes the RBA is walking a fine line: acknowledge progress without letting people think the fight is over. Rates are on hold for now, but the RBA won't be cutting quickly either.

ai.summary: The biggest AI story of the week is a remarkable one — over a thousand employees at the world's top AI labs are calling on the US government to pump the brakes on their own technology. Separately, Sam Altman was in Congress discussing how to regulate AI.

stories.title: 1,100 AI insiders call for slowdown — including staff at OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta and Google
stories.why_it_matters: More than 1,100 researchers and engineers at OpenAI, Anthropic, Google and Meta have signed an open letter asking the US government to introduce rules that slow down AI development — specifically AI systems that can improve and rewrite themselves without human oversight. OpenAI and Anthropic formally backed the proposal. This is unusual: the very companies racing to build the most powerful AI are now asking for guardrails. The concern is that once AI can write better AI, development could accelerate beyond human control. For investors in GOOG and AI-linked holdings like GXAI, it signals that regulation is coming and could reshape the competitive landscape.

stories.title: OpenAI and Anthropic formally back plan to slow AI that writes its own code
stories.why_it_matters: OpenAI and Anthropic have put their institutional weight behind a proposal to slow down 'recursive self-improvement' in AI — the process where AI systems write better versions of themselves, potentially without meaningful human oversight. This is notable because both companies are simultaneously racing each other to release the most capable models. It suggests even the most bullish AI developers are genuinely uncertain about what happens when AI gets very good at improving itself. The proposal is now in front of US Congress, with Sam Altman briefing lawmakers directly this week.

stories.title: Sam Altman visits Congress to discuss AI regulation
stories.why_it_matters: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman headed to Capitol Hill this week to brief US lawmakers on AI development and the case for regulation. His visit coincides with the employee letter and growing calls for the government to set rules before AI becomes too powerful to easily constrain. Congress is now under real pressure from both the industry and its own workers to act — whatever framework emerges will shape how companies like Google, Microsoft and OpenAI operate for years to come.

stories.title: Trump reviews AI regulations — balancing development against China competition
stories.why_it_matters: The Trump administration is reviewing existing AI regulations with an eye on the US-China technology competition. The concern in the White House is that heavy-handed rules could slow American AI companies while Chinese rivals like DeepSeek race ahead unconstrained. This creates a genuine tension: the AI industry wants guardrails, employees are demanding slowdowns, but the government is worried that slowing down could hand China a strategic advantage. How this gets resolved will be one of the defining policy debates of the next few years.

sport.summary: NRL Round 22 kicks off tonight with Cowboys vs Roosters, while the Broncos have lost a premiership-winning prop to medical retirement. AFL has big selection news heading into a top-six clash, and young Cruz Hewitt is making tennis headlines.

stories.title: Broncos premiership prop Corey Jensen retires due to blood clots
stories.why_it_matters: Brisbane Broncos prop Corey Jensen, who was part of the Broncos' premiership-winning squad, has been forced into medical retirement due to recurring blood clots. Jensen is just 26. The Broncos confirmed the news on Thursday, with the club paying tribute to his contribution. It's a tough blow for Jensen personally and leaves the Broncos short of experienced front-row depth as they head into the business end of the season — they host the Knights on Saturday night at Suncorp Stadium.

stories.title: Major blow for Panthers as Titans reportedly sign two players from Penrith
stories.why_it_matters: The Gold Coast Titans have reportedly secured signatures from two players currently contracted to the Penrith Panthers for 2027. The Panthers, who have dominated the NRL for several years, are facing a significant talent drain as rival clubs pick off their depth players. The specific names weren't confirmed in the report, but it's being described as a 'major blow' for Penrith's roster planning. Meanwhile, the Titans host the Warriors at Cbus Super Stadium on Saturday at 3pm — a chance for the local team to build some momentum.

stories.title: Tom Dearden considered shock move to Sydney before staying in Queensland
stories.why_it_matters: Cowboys halfback Tom Dearden was apparently weighing up a shock move to a Sydney club before ultimately deciding to stay in Queensland. Fox Sports reports the details of the approach, though the specific club wasn't named. Dearden is one of the best halves in the competition and his retention is a big deal for North Queensland — he plays tonight as the Cowboys host the Roosters at Queensland Country Bank Stadium (7:50pm AEST) in the Round 22 opener.

stories.title: AFL: Geelong make shock call on star, Collingwood get major early return for top-six clash
stories.why_it_matters: Geelong made a surprise selection call on a key player ahead of a crucial top-six eliminator, while Collingwood received good news with a star player returning earlier than expected from injury. The Daicos-Mullin match-up is being flagged as potentially decisive — Nick Daicos (Collingwood) against Geelong's Luke Mullin shapes as one of the most important midfield battles of the AFL season so far. With finals positioning on the line, this game has significant ladder implications for both clubs.

stories.title: Cruz Hewitt 'on the brink of exploding' — inside the rise of Lleyton's son
stories.why_it_matters: Fox Sports has a detailed profile on Cruz Hewitt, son of Australian tennis legend Lleyton, describing him as being 'on the brink of exploding' onto the professional tennis scene. The piece addresses some 'ugly claims' about his rise that apparently need to be reckoned with, while detailing the remarkable trajectory of a young player with serious pedigree. For Australian tennis fans, Cruz represents a potential next chapter in the Hewitt family's contribution to the sport.
